app.name: Mercury API OAuth integration (your own partner client)

verdict.summary: Mercury has no self-serve OAuth developer console. You cannot create a client yourself: you submit a partner intake form and wait for Mercury to issue a client ID, secret and test-client credentials, with no published review window. Once approved, the OAuth setup itself is standard (PKCE, exact redirect URI match, refresh tokens), and no money-moving OAuth scope exists, so payment products must use per-customer API tokens instead.
verdict.hands_on_effort: About 2-4 hours of active work (form, redirect and policy links, OAuth flow test), spread around an unknown approval wait
verdict.time_to_first_connection: Unknown. Starts only after Mercury approves the partner request; no timeline is published
verdict.approval_wait: Unknown. Mercury says timelines vary with integration complexity, security, use-case fit and regulatory factors, and publishes no fixed window

limits: No self-serve OAuth developer console; Mercury issues credentials after a request

gates.time_to_reach: Form submission takes under an hour; approval time unknown

gates.name: Sandbox test client (after approval)

Per-endpoint rate limits are not published
No money-moving OAuth scope; payment products need per-customer API tokens

steps.title: Decide whether you need partner OAuth at all
steps.detail: Partner OAuth is only needed if your product acts for other Mercury customers. If you only automate your own Mercury workspace, use an API token from the Mercury dashboard instead. Any multi-tenant product that sends payments should plan for per-customer API tokens, because no OAuth scope moves money.
gotchas: API token creation is controlled by an admin on the Mercury account, usually the account owner or beneficial owner

steps.title: Confirm there is no Composio managed app to start from
steps.detail: Composio's toolkit lookup for 'mercury' returned nothing, so there is no managed OAuth app and no default scope list. Plan on registering your own Mercury OAuth client through the partner process.

steps.title: Draft the partner intake form answers
steps.detail: Draft answers for the intake form fields: company name and website, postal address, a short company description, the product being connected, and the intended API use. Keep the API use list to the specific endpoints and scopes you need (read, offline_access, and any MCP write scopes only if required).
gotchas: The Notion page linked from the OAuth docs did not load during research; the field list was taken from the docs page, so check the live form for extra questions

steps.title: Submit the partner OAuth intake form
steps.detail: Open the integrations OAuth page and submit the approval request with the drafted answers. Mercury may ask about account prerequisites, which are not documented (for example a paid plan, EIN or business verification); confirm these before you submit.
gotchas: No self-serve developer console exists, so there is no app to create in advance
Mercury does not publish a review window

steps.title: Wait for Mercury to approve and issue credentials
steps.detail: Mercury weighs security, use-case fit and regulatory factors. There is no published timeline, so ask Mercury for an expected date if you need one. Do not start production work until the client ID and secret arrive.

steps.title: Supply a GPG public key to receive credentials
steps.detail: Mercury requires a GPG public key so it can deliver the client ID, client secret and test-client credentials securely. Generate a key pair if you do not have one and send the public key as part of the post-approval setup.

steps.title: Register redirect URIs on the client
steps.detail: Register your production redirect URI and any dev/test redirect URIs with Mercury. The redirect_uri sent during authorization must exactly match one of these registered URLs, including scheme, host, path and trailing slash. Paste the exact callback URL from your Composio auth config.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Any mismatch, including a trailing slash, causes the authorize request to fail

steps.title: Configure the authorization request
steps.detail: Build the authorize request to the partner endpoint with response_type=code, a PKCE code_challenge using method S256, a state value of at least eight characters, and a space-separated scope list. Request offline_access in the request as well as in the client configuration if you need access without the user present.

values.label: scope
values.value: read offline_access (plus any approved write scopes)

steps.title: Run a sandbox authorization with the test client
steps.detail: Using the sandbox test-client credentials, run the full flow: authorize, exchange the code for tokens, call a read endpoint, then refresh the token. Confirm the authorize step rejects unknown client IDs before login, as Mercury's endpoint does.
gotchas: Expect invalid_client if the client ID is wrong or not yet issued

steps.title: Implement token refresh with single-use refresh tokens
steps.detail: Store the new refresh token returned on every refresh, because each refresh token works only once. Refresh access tokens before the one-hour expiry. Plan for re-authorization when a refresh token passes its 720-hour lifetime.
gotchas: Reusing an old refresh token after a successful refresh will fail
Refresh tokens lapse after 720 hours and the user must sign in again

steps.title: Decide on write scopes and user consent
steps.detail: Only request write scopes you need. Mercury's MCP docs require the specific write scope to be listed and the user to consent. Payments and transfers from the MCP create requests that a person must approve in Mercury, so design your product to match that approval step.

steps.title: Add terms, privacy policy and logo links
steps.detail: Provide links to your app's terms of service, privacy policy and logo as part of the post-approval setup. The agent can draft the privacy policy and terms, but you must publish them on a site you control and review them with counsel.
gotchas: Links must be live before submission; Mercury's requirements for content are not further specified in the docs

steps.title: Move to production credentials and go live
steps.detail: Once Mercury issues the production client, swap the sandbox client ID and secret for production, confirm the production redirect URI, and re-run the authorization test. No separate marketplace or listing review is documented, but confirm this with Mercury before public launch.

requirements.detail: Submit company name and website, postal address, company description, the product being connected, and intended API use. Approval is required before any client ID or secret is issued.
Register a production redirect URI and optional dev/test redirect URIs. The authorize request must exactly match one of them.
Provide a GPG public key so Mercury can deliver the client ID, secret and test-client credentials.
Authorize requests use response_type=code and code_challenge_method=S256.
Access tokens last one hour. Refresh tokens are single-use, return a new refresh token on each refresh, and lapse after 720 hours.

requirements.item: Terms of service, privacy policy and logo links
requirements.detail: Links to your terms, privacy policy and logo are required as part of the post-approval setup.
Docs describe the partner approval as the only gate. No public listing or app-store review was found. This is not independently verified.

scopes.effect: Read access for read tools. Only documented in third-party analysis for the API, so confirm it on your approved client. Mercury publishes no sensitive or restricted tier for OAuth scopes.
Needed to keep access when the user is not present. Must be set in the client configuration and when starting the flow.

scopes.scope: Specific MCP write scopes (listed in Mercury's MCP docs)
scopes.effect: Each write scope requires explicit user consent. Payment and transfer actions create requests that a person must approve in Mercury. Partner-API write scopes are not documented, so confirm them with Mercury before requesting.

blockers.symptom: Cannot create an OAuth app or get a client ID; the docs say OAuth access requires prior approval.
blockers.cause: Mercury has no self-serve OAuth developer console. Credentials are issued only after the partner intake form is approved.
blockers.fix: Submit the partner intake form at the OAuth integrations page and wait. For single-workspace use, use an API token instead.

blockers.symptom: No timeline for approval; the docs say only that it varies.
blockers.cause: Mercury weighs integration complexity, security, use-case fit and regulatory factors and publishes no fixed window.
blockers.fix: Plan around an unknown wait. Ask Mercury for an expected date, and do not commit a launch date until credentials arrive.

blockers.symptom: Payments cannot be sent through the OAuth flow; no scope in the docs moves money.
blockers.cause: No documented OAuth scope can move money. Third-party analysis says payment products need per-customer API tokens.
blockers.fix: For multi-tenant payments, use per-customer API tokens created by each customer's account admin. Keep OAuth for read and consented actions.

blockers.cause: The client ID does not exist or is not yet issued. The endpoint rejects unknown clients before login.
blockers.fix: Confirm the client ID from the approved credentials delivery. Do not use placeholder IDs.

blockers.symptom: Authorization fails with a redirect URI error.
blockers.cause: The redirect_uri sent does not exactly match a URL registered to the client.
blockers.fix: Paste the exact Composio callback URL into the registered redirect URIs and match it character for character in the request.

blockers.cause: On the MCP dynamic-registration path, a client_name that begins with the word Mercury causes registration to fail.
blockers.fix: Use a client name that does not start with Mercury. This applies only to the MCP path, not the partner API path.

blockers.symptom: Rate limits are unclear; no per-endpoint limits are documented.
blockers.cause: Mercury does not publish per-endpoint rate limits, per third-party analysis.
blockers.fix: Build backoff and caching into the integration and confirm limits with Mercury during approval.

composio.note: Composio has no Mercury toolkit, so there is no managed OAuth app to start from and no default scopes. You must register your own Mercury partner client, which requires Mercury's approval first. Mercury's hosted MCP server supports dynamic client registration without approval, but that path is for MCP clients, not the partner API OAuth path used here.

evidence.claim: Partner OAuth against Mercury's API is gated behind an advance sign-off, so a developer cannot self-enable it.
evidence.quote: OAuth access to Mercury’s API requires prior approval.

evidence.claim: The partner authorize endpoint is on the oauth2.mercury.com host, and the request takes client_id, redirect_uri, a space-separated scope list, and a state value of at least eight characters.
evidence.quote: get https://oauth2.mercury.com/oauth2/auth

evidence.claim: Access tokens expire after one hour; to keep access without the user present, the offline_access scope must be set both in the client configuration and when starting the flow.
evidence.quote: For security reasons, the access token expires in one hour.

evidence.claim: Each refresh token works only once, and every successful refresh returns a new refresh token alongside the access token. Refresh tokens lapse 720 hours after issue, after which the user must re-authorize.
evidence.quote: A refresh token expires in 720 hours.

evidence.claim: A third-party analysis counts only two OAuth scopes in Mercury's API docs, read and offline_access, and says write capability is described through API token scopes instead.
evidence.quote: Mercury documents only two OAuth scopes: read and offline_access.

evidence.claim: Mercury's MCP docs tell clients to request read for read tools and to ask for specific write scopes, each requiring user consent.
evidence.quote: For write actions, request the specific scopes listed below and obtain the user's consent.

evidence.claim: Payment and transfer write actions from the MCP only create requests that a person must approve in Mercury, while category and note edits take effect immediately.
evidence.quote: Requires approval in Mercury before money is sent.

evidence.claim: Per a third-party analysis, no OAuth scope in Mercury's docs can move money, so a multi-tenant product that sends payments must use per-customer API tokens.
evidence.quote: There is no documented OAuth scope that moves money.

evidence.claim: Mercury's getting-started guide describes a read-only API token that needs no IP allowlist, and a custom token limited to RequestSendMoney for queuing payments that require admin approval. Both suit a single-owner setup, not a multi-tenant OAuth app.
evidence.quote: Does not require an IP whitelist.

evidence.claim: Creating API tokens is limited to users with the right permission; an admin on the account, usually the person who set up the account or its beneficial owner, controls it.
evidence.quote: This is a setting that can be fully controlled by an admin from your company

evidence.claim: The intake form asks for the company's name and website, its postal address, a short company description, the product being connected, and the intended API use.
evidence.quote: Your company name and website

evidence.claim: The MCP server supports RFC 7591 dynamic client registration, so an MCP client gets its own client_id at runtime and nobody has to pre-approve it.
evidence.quote: Your client asks Mercury for its own credentials at runtime. Nobody has to create an app for you first.

evidence.claim: On the MCP dynamic-registration path, any client name starting with the word Mercury makes registration fail.
evidence.quote: The client_name must not begin with the word "Mercury", or registration fails

evidence.claim: No app-store, marketplace, or public-listing review exists for Mercury OAuth apps in the docs; the only documented gate is the partner approval form. Pages checked: integrations-with-oauth2, startoauth2flow, obtain-the-tokens, getting-started, security-best-practices, and the MCP guides.

The security best-practices page covers user-side safety for the MCP (least-privilege permissions, reviewing clients, revocation) and does not set any app-vetting or security-assessment requirement for developers.
evidence.quote: The ability to revoke access at any time from your Mercury dashboard

evidence.claim: No install cap, user limit, or unreviewed-app limit for Mercury OAuth apps turned up in the docs or searches. Third-party analysis says per-endpoint rate limits are not published.
evidence.quote: per endpoint rate limits go unpublished.

evidence.claim: A probe with a made-up client_id got a standard OAuth invalid_client error from the live authorize endpoint, so the endpoint checks clients before any login.
evidence.quote: The requested OAuth 2.0 Client does not exist.

evidence.claim: The probe of the docs root landed on a reference page behind a login wall, and the docs site links to the API reference, Guides and Changelog. No separate partner console was found.
evidence.quote: For AI agents: the docs index is at https://docs.mercury.com/llms.txt.

evidence.claim: Mercury says approval time depends on integration complexity and weighs security, use-case fit and regulatory factors; it publishes no fixed review window.
evidence.quote: Approval timelines vary depending on integration complexity

evidence.claim: A third-party integrator notes that Mercury gives no self-serve OAuth developer console; the developer submits a request and waits for Mercury to issue credentials.
evidence.quote: Mercury does not offer a self-serve developer console for OAuth.

evidence.claim: Supergood's guide limits the approval gate to products that act for other Mercury customers; a company working only inside its own Mercury workspace can use an API token.
evidence.quote: The OAuth2 approval form is only needed when building integrations consumed by other Mercury customers

evidence.claim: Once a client exists, Mercury delivers the client ID and secret securely and also issues sandbox test-client credentials.
evidence.quote: we will securely share your client ID and client secret as well as credentials for a test client

evidence.claim: The post-approval setup requires a production redirect URI, optional dev/test redirect URIs, links to terms of service, privacy policy and logo, and a GPG public key used to deliver credentials.
evidence.quote: Links to your app’s terms of service, privacy policy, and logo

evidence.claim: The redirect_uri sent at authorization must exactly match one of the URLs registered to the client.
evidence.quote: Must match one of the URLs registered with the client.

evidence.claim: The authorize request uses the PKCE code challenge method S256, with response_type code.
evidence.quote: Must have value S256, the SHA256 function used to hash the code challenge.
